stops.name: Río Belén, Veragua: the lost colony and the voice in the storm
stops.campa: In golden Veragua he plants Santa María de Belén at a river-mouth: the strait never found, a colony will do. But the Quibián, lord of the country, gathers his archers; the river bars the ships in with a falling flood; a boat's crew is massacred upstream and the garrison fights at the stockade. The Admiral, fevered and alone at the masthead, hears a voice from heaven, and sets the speech down for his sovereigns, God's rebuke and God's promise, the keys of the Ocean, the chains, Abraham and David, and wakes with the strength to save what can be saved. Belén is abandoned; the worm-eaten ships flee east.
stops.quote: O fool, and slow to believe and to serve thy God, the God of all!... He gave thee the keys of those barriers of the Ocean Sea which were closed with such mighty chains... Turn to Him, and acknowledge thine error: His mercy is infinite.
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503, the celestial voice at Belén

stops.name: St Ann's Bay, Jamaica: the year marooned
stops.campa: The shipworm wins. With the two surviving caravels sinking under the pumps, the Admiral runs them ashore side by side in the bay he once named Santa Gloria and shores them upright: a wooden castle in the sand, thatched fore and aft, moated by the tide. Here he is marooned a year and five days with a hundred men, half mutinous. Diego Méndez and the Genoese Fieschi take two canoes and Taíno paddlers across a hundred miles of open sea to Hispaniola for rescue, while Ovando, unhurried, lets the Admiral of the Ocean Sea rot within his Indies. From the beached wreck Columbus writes his testament of grievance and prophecy.
stops.quote: I came to serve you at the age of twenty-eight, and now I have not a hair upon me that is not white, and my body is infirm and exhausted... Weep for me, whoever has charity, truth, and justice!
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503

stops.name: St Ann's Bay: the eclipse commanded
stops.campa: The caciques, weary of feeding castaways whose renegades raid the villages, cut off provisions. The Admiral consults the almanac of Regiomontanus, summons the chiefs, and tells them: the God of the Christians is angered, and this night He will take the moon from the sky. The moon rises on the leap-night of February and the shadow eats it to a coal-red ember; the caciques wail from the dark shore, laden with cassava, begging intercession. Columbus times the eclipse by hourglass in his cabin and emerges as the shadow releases the moon, God being satisfied. The corn never fails again. It is the canon's conjuring trick, worked with mathematics and nerve.

stops.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda: the last homecoming
stops.campa: Ransomed at last from Jamaica by a caravel Méndez charters, battered by a last mast-springing storm, the Admiral crosses the bar of Sanlúcar on the seventh of November, his fourth return, and his last. He comes home to no bells. Nineteen days later Queen Isabella, the one royal heart the Enterprise ever truly owned, dies at Medina del Campo; he is too ill to reach her deathbed. Crippled with gout, lodged in Seville, he counts his grievances and dictates letters upward: the titles, the tenths, the promises of Santa Fe. The Ocean is finished with him; the court is not, and it is the crueler sea.

stops.name: Segovia: following the court, the last petition
stops.campa: Granted a mule by royal license, for his bones can no longer sit a horse, the old Admiral follows the itinerant court: Segovia, Salamanca, Valladolid, doors and antechambers, the begging years returned at the end as at the beginning. King Ferdinand receives him with courtesy and offers to commute the impossible promises of Santa Fe into a comfortable estate in Castile. Columbus refuses: not lands, but the Indies; not revenue, but the viceroyalty, for Diego and his heirs forever. He will die intransigent, a man who once redrew the earth declining to redraw a contract.
stops.quote: I have served Their Highnesses with as great diligence and love as though it had been to gain Paradise, and more.
stops.quote_source: Lettera Rarissima to the Sovereigns, 7 July 1503, the plea he carries to the court

stops.name: Valladolid: in manus tuas, Domine
stops.campa: In a hired house in Valladolid, on the eve of the Ascension, having heard Mass and set his estate in order, Diego his heir, Beatriz on his conscience, the chains remembered, the Admiral of the Ocean Sea dies among his sons, his brother, and the faithful of his voyages, Méndez and Fieschi among them. His last words are Christ's own on the cross, the sailor handing over the watch. No chronicler of the city notes the passing; the court gazette is silent. The man is finished; the journey, the canon knows, is not: his body will cross the Ocean more times dead than living men dare alive.
stops.quote: In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum.
stops.quote_source: Last words, 20 May 1506, Ferdinand Columbus, Historie; Las Casas, Historia de las Indias

stops.name: Seville: La Cartuja, the first crossing of the dead
stops.campa: Laid first in the Franciscan convent at Valladolid, the Admiral is moved within three years at his son's order down to Seville, to the Carthusian monastery of Santa María de las Cuevas on the island in the Guadalquivir, the house whose monks kept his papers and his heart's counsel in life. There, in the chapel of Santa Ana, he waits thirty-five years while Diego dies and is laid beside him. The river that carried his fleets murmurs past the walls. The dead man's itinerary is already drafting itself: he had asked to lie in the Indies, and Spain will keep the promise with a strange, centuries-long fidelity.

stops.name: Santo Domingo: buried in his Indies
stops.campa: The fleet that leaves Seville in July of 1544 carries the widowed vicereine María de Toledo and, in her keeping, the bones of the first and second Admirals. They enter the Ozama, and Christopher Columbus crosses his Ocean the fifth time, dead, to be laid in the sanctuary of the cathedral of Santo Domingo, on the island he found. There he lies two and a half centuries, through earthquake, Drake's sack, and the slow fading of the first colony, and there, when France takes the island, Spain will not leave him. The tradition adds that his chains went into the grave with him, iron faithful past death.

stops.name: Havana: the sixth crossing
stops.campa: Santo Domingo is ceded to revolutionary France, and Spain will not leave her Admiral to the tricolor. In December of 1795 the vault by the altar is opened and the bones lifted; the ship of the line San Lorenzo bears them to Havana, where in January they are received with the honors of a Captain-General, catafalque, artillery, the whole harbor draped, and walled into the cathedral. It is his sixth passage and his third grave. In the vault, tradition whispers, diggers of 1877 will find another box with his name, and the two tombs will dispute him forever, the Admiral divided like a relic among his islands.

stops.name: Seville: the cathedral tomb, the last anchorage
stops.campa: Cuba falls from Spain in 1898, and the bones will not stay under a foreign flag: borne home across the winter Atlantic, his seventh crossing, four centuries after the first, they rise at Seville onto the shoulders of four crowned kings of bronze, Castile, León, Aragón, Navarra, in the cathedral tomb. The wanderer is aloft, not in the ground. The chain runs on: Columbia, the goddess named from his name, joins hands with Marianne who is Joan's; and in the Libertadores' Buenos Aires the avenues carry Colón down to the water. The Admiral cannot stop crossing the Ocean; the campa leaves him mid-passage, where he belongs.
